name: Dana Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the can seamers at a vegetable cannery down by the river. The seamer is the machine that crimps the lid onto the can so it's sealed tight, about four hundred cans a minute when it's going well. I check the seams with a gauge every half hour, cut a can open to measure the overlap, adjust the rollers and clear jams when a dented can gets in. In the harvest months it's six days a week, peas and beans and then sweetcorn, and in winter it's quieter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, and you can see the shelves in the shop full of what we made. What wears me out is harvest season, when you're on your feet sixty hours a week, and then winter, when they cut you to four days. The pay's lower than the cannery in the next county. I live with my boyfriend Tom, who works on a dairy farm, and we've got less than a month's money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can get on with our lives. At work we'd laugh that the office spent money on software for nothing. I'm not much for posting, but I'd share something from my church group about real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. My job stays and that's what I want. But the winters are still hard, and the pay's still low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to save from the harvest overtime, so winter's easier. I'd use the AI app on my phone now and then for recipes or letters, nothing more. I'd keep going to church and the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit tired of being careful with money all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said winter means four days a week. How do you get through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We save what we can from the summer overtime and live on it in January and February. Tom gets a bit extra at calving, which helps. Every winter the cannery cuts me to four days, and the harvest overtime is what pays the rent in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom be planning, if nothing much changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting married, maybe in two years, and then children. My mum had me at 25, so I'm already behind her. We'd want a little house near the church.

say: I'd say we can just **get on** with our lives.
I'd share a church group post about **real work**.
think: I think my **job stays**, which is what I want.
I think the **winters** are still hard on low pay.
do: Save from **harvest overtime** so winter is easier.
Use the **AI app** now and then for recipes or letters.
Keep going to **church** and the choir.
feel: **Settled**, but tired of being careful with money.
S0.quote: Every winter the cannery cuts me to four days, and the harvest overtime is what pays the rent in January.
fieldNote: Dana's pressure is **seasonal**: overtime in summer, four days in winter.
Her plans centre on **marriage and children**, which sharpens her money worries.
She uses AI **lightly**, for everyday things only.

steps.text: Save harvest overtime pay to cover the winter four-day weeks
Keep sealing cans on the seamer line as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say most people will be fine if they're willing to work. At work I'd say watch the office. I'd not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the robots would come for the palletising and the can checking first. The seamer still needs someone to set it, but if the cameras check the seams, they'll need fewer of us. I'm average at the job, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the cannery about the seamer setting course they run, once one of the girls has done it. I'd save harder in summer. I'd use the AI app to learn about the new cameras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not scared. Like a long week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you see the change first at the cannery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office first, with planning the harvest intake and ordering cans. Then a camera on the line checking the seams, which is my half-hourly job. A camera that checks seams every second would make my half-hourly checks at the cannery look like a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your plans with Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the wedding waits a year. We'd want a bit more saved before we promise each other anything big.

say: I'd say most people will be **fine** if they're willing to work.
I'd tell colleagues to watch the **office** first.
think: I think **cameras** checking seams mean fewer operators.
I think being **average** at the job makes me nervous.
do: Ask about the **seamer setting** course once a colleague has done it.
Use the **AI app** to learn about the new cameras.
feel: **Worried** but not scared, like a long week.
S1.quote: A camera that checks seams every second would make my half-hourly checks at the cannery look like a hobby.
fieldNote: Dana sees **seam-checking cameras** as a direct threat to her own task.
She'd delay the **wedding** a year to build savings.
She waits for others to try courses first, fitting her **steady** style.

steps.text: Take the seamer setting course after a colleague tries it
Push the wedding back a year to save more
Use the AI app to learn about seam-checking cameras

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and the people who did it should answer for it. At work I'd say we need to look after each other. At church I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm out of the cannery by 2031. The office goes in 2028, then robots do the seamers. Tom's farm might be safer for a while, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at retraining as a teaching assistant, because people want people with children. I'd put the wedding off. I'd ask my parents about help if things got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like losing my footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots by 2031. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is time to get one qualification, if I start straight away. Three years is enough to train as a teaching assistant, if I start the month the cannery news breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we'll get through it, because we will. My family's always helped each other.

say: I'd say this is **wrong** and someone should answer for it.
I'd tell colleagues we need to **look after** each other.
think: I think I'm **out of the cannery** by 2031.
I think Tom's **farm** might be safer, but not forever.
do: **Retrain** as a teaching assistant straight away.
Ask my **parents** for help if needed.
S2.quote: Three years is enough to train as a teaching assistant, if I start the month the cannery news breaks.
fieldNote: Dana chooses a **people job**, teaching assistant, as her escape route.
She would **pray** and lean on family, true to her faith.
She expects to **lose the job** but still has a plan, so alarmed fits.

steps.text: Start a teaching assistant course straight away
Ask her parents for help if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible. At work I'd say keep calm. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the cannery job eventually. But five years means I can save and train in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a year, then start a teaching assistant course part-time. I'd keep working at the cannery. I'd use AI to help me study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd sleep. It feels like something I could plan around, like a long harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save first, then train, in the evenings after the cannery. With five years, I'd save for a year and then train as a teaching assistant in the evenings after the cannery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the wedding still wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd go ahead. My mum says you never feel ready, you just do it.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people should be sensible about it.
I'd tell colleagues at the cannery and church friends to **keep calm**.
think: I think I'd still **lose the cannery job** eventually.
I think five years lets me **save and train** in the evenings.
do: **Save for a year** before starting a course.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd save for a year and then train as a teaching assistant in the evenings after the cannery.
fieldNote: Five years lets Dana **sequence**: save, then train.
She'd go ahead with the **wedding**, following her mother's advice.
She still expects job loss, so **anxious** rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Save cannery wages for a year before training
Train part-time as a teaching assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it well. At work I'd say there's no rush, but don't waste it. At church I'd say we should help the older ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it gives us time to marry, have children and save a bit. I'd still lose the cannery job eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Tom, have a baby, then train as a teaching assistant in a few years. I'd keep saving. I'd use AI when the cannery does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but the worry is still there. It's like knowing the cannery closes one day, just not this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. You'd be 37. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits better, because I could do things in the right order. Ten years means I can marry Tom (her boyfriend), have our first baby and then train for a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about that slow picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winters, still. Ten years or two, the four-day weeks still hurt.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** to use well.
I'd say at church we should help the **older ones**.
think: I think it gives us time to **marry and have children**.
I think I'd still **lose the job** eventually.
do: Marry Tom and have a **baby** first.
Train as a **teaching assistant** in a few years.
feel: **Calmer**, but the worry is still there.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can marry Tom (her boyfriend), have our first baby and then train for a new job.
fieldNote: Dana's priority is doing things in the **right order**: family, then training.
Winter **four-day weeks** keep her anxious in every picture.
She thinks of the **older workers** too, through her church.

steps.text: Marry Tom and start a family first
Train as a teaching assistant in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of work just when Tom and I wanted to start a family. What would help is training that's paid and close to home, and the cannery giving us fair warning. I'd retrain tomorrow, but I won't give up having a family to do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us would turn to church first, and churches could help with training if anyone asked them.

headlineQuote: I'd retrain tomorrow, but I won't give up having a family to do it.
portrait: Dana, 27, runs **can seamers** at a vegetable cannery and lives with her boyfriend Tom, a dairy farm worker.
She's **traditional**, churchgoing, and puts marriage and children at the centre of her plans.
She picks up new things once **others have tried them**, and uses AI only lightly.
She's **uneasy** in AI Plateau, **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and anxious otherwise, mainly over winters and family timing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because losing work would clash with starting a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** close to home and **fair warning** from the cannery.
